groups.high: Pew Research Center's analysis of US median hourly earnings for full- and part-time workers found that women earned about 85% of men's earnings in 2024. This is an aggregate, unadjusted comparison, not a finding that every woman receives 85 cents for identical work. BLS weekly earnings and Census annual earnings use different populations and measures and should not be treated as interchangeable. Occupational sorting, hours, experience, caregiving interruptions, promotion opportunities, and discrimination can contribute to observed differences. Care responsibilities and the motherhood penalty can affect paid hours, career continuity, and progression; effects vary between groups. Statistical adjustment can describe some differences but cannot by itself identify the causal contribution of discrimination or show that all controlled factors are free from structural inequality. Pay transparency, equitable hiring and promotion, accessible childcare, and caregiving policies are possible responses whose effects require evaluation. A national average can hide differences by age, race, occupation, and parenthood. Comparing definitions, periods, and populations is essential before interpreting changes or deciding whether a particular employer pays fairly.
groups.mid: Pew Research Center found that women earned about 85% of what men earned in the US in 2024, using median hourly pay for full- and part-time workers. This is an overall comparison, not proof that each woman gets 85 cents for doing the same job as a man. BLS weekly pay figures and Census yearly pay figures use different measures and groups. You cannot swap them without checking. The gap can reflect the jobs people hold, hours, experience, care work, access to promotions, and discrimination. Time out to care for children can affect paid hours, job progress, and later earnings. This is sometimes called the motherhood penalty, but its size varies. A study can adjust for some differences. It cannot use that alone to prove how much is caused by discrimination, or that every factor is fair. Clear pay information, fair hiring and promotion, affordable childcare, and support for carers may help. Their results need to be tested. A national average can hide gaps by age, race, job, and parenthood. Check the measure, year, and people included before judging progress or one employer's pay.
groups.low: Pew Research Center compared hourly pay in the US in 2024. It used the median, or middle value, for full- and part-time workers. Women's pay was about 85% of men's. This does not mean every woman gets 85 cents for the same work a man does for a dollar. BLS weekly pay and Census yearly pay figures count different things and groups. Check before comparing them. Pay gaps can reflect jobs, hours, skills gained at work, care duties, promotions, and unfair treatment. Time out to care for a child can slow pay growth or a career. This is called the motherhood penalty, and its size varies, while a study may account for some differences. That alone cannot show how much unfair treatment caused the gap. It also cannot prove that every factor is fair. Clear pay ranges, fair hiring and promotion, affordable childcare, and help for carers may help. We must check their effects. One national figure can hide gaps by age, race, job, or parenthood. Check the year, group, and pay measure before judging change or an employer's fairness.
groups.source_review: Checked Pew 2024 hourly-pay measure and discussion of contributing factors. Did not infer a same-job causal effect from the aggregate ratio.
groups.notes: Separated incompatible pay measures and removed deterministic causal claims.

groups.high: UNHCR's Global Trends 2024 reported approximately 123.2 million forcibly displaced people at the end of 2024. This historical total includes people displaced within their own countries as well as refugees, asylum-seekers, and other specified protection categories; it is not a count of refugees alone. Low- and middle-income countries hosted about 73% of refugees under the report's stated classification, not 73% of every displaced category. Large arrivals can increase demand for housing, schools, healthcare, and public infrastructure, particularly where resources are already limited. Outcomes also depend on support, rights, investment, and opportunities for refugees to work and contribute. Displacement should not be described as an inevitable economic loss or source of conflict. The 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol do exist, although participation and protection in practice are uneven. Effective responses include protection against return to danger, fair asylum procedures, support for host communities, humanitarian financing, and durable solutions such as voluntary safe return, local integration, or resettlement where appropriate. Refugee and host-community needs should be assessed together rather than assuming they are inherently opposed.
groups.mid: UNHCR's Global Trends 2024 counted about 123.2 million forcibly displaced people at the end of 2024. This includes people who fled within their own country. It also includes refugees, people seeking asylum, and other groups needing protection. It is not a count of refugees alone. Low- and middle-income countries hosted about 73% of refugees in the report's measure. That is not 73% of all displaced people. Large arrivals can add pressure on homes, schools, health services, and roads, especially where services are already stretched. But refugees can also work and contribute if they have rights and support. The outcome depends on policy, funding, and local conditions; harm or conflict is not inevitable. There is an international refugee treaty: the 1951 Refugee Convention, with its 1967 Protocol. Not all countries take part, and protection can still fail. Responses should stop people being sent back to danger, provide fair asylum decisions, fund aid, and help host communities. Longer-term options include a safe, willing return, settling locally, or resettling elsewhere where suitable. Assess both groups' needs instead of treating refugees and hosts as natural rivals.
groups.low: UNHCR's Global Trends 2024 counted about 123.2 million people forced from home by the end of 2024. Some stayed inside their own country. Others were refugees, people seeking asylum, or in other protection groups. They were not all refugees. Low- and middle-income countries hosted about 73% of refugees in the report's measure. This is not 73% of all people forced from home. Many new arrivals can put pressure on homes, schools, health care, and roads. This is harder where services are already short of funds. But refugees can work and help their new community if they have rights and support. The result depends on funding, policy, and the place. It need not cause conflict or economic loss. A world refugee treaty does exist: the 1951 Refugee Convention and its 1967 Protocol. Not all countries join or protect people well in practice. People must not be sent back to danger. They need fair asylum decisions, aid, and support for host communities. Lasting options may be a safe, willing return home, settling locally, or moving to a third country where suitable. Check both hosts' and refugees' needs. Do not assume one group must lose for the other to gain.
groups.source_review: Checked UNHCR historical displacement totals, hosting share, and treaty framework.
groups.notes: Corrected denial of global refugee treaty and displaced/refugee category confusion; removed unsupported universal economic-burden claims.

groups.high: WHO's World Mental Health Report 2022 described approximately one in eight people worldwide living with a mental disorder in 2019. This is not the same as one in four adults at a particular time or lifetime risk. Treatment gaps vary by condition, country, and definition; the report does not justify a universal statement that only 10% of every low-income patient group receives evidence-based care. Cost, scarce trained staff, distance, stigma, discrimination, and services poorly adapted to language or culture can impede access. Poverty can increase exposure to stress and reduce access to care, while mental illness can disrupt education, work, and income. These relationships do not justify treating all low-income people as ill, dangerous, or incapable. Evidence-based care uses the best available research together with clinical judgment and the person's needs and preferences. Appropriate psychological, social, and medication options differ by condition. Improving community services, integrating care with general healthcare, protecting rights, addressing stigma, and sustainable financing can narrow gaps. Claims that clinicians routinely dismiss symptoms as a named poverty syndrome or that most patients receive placebo treatments require evidence and should not be assumed.
groups.mid: WHO's World Mental Health Report 2022 said about one in eight people worldwide had a mental disorder in 2019. This is not the same as saying one in four adults has one now or over a lifetime. The share who get care varies by illness, country, and how care is defined. There is no single proven rule that only 10% of all low-income patients get evidence-based treatment. Barriers include cost, too few trained staff, travel, stigma, unfair treatment, and care that does not fit a person's language or culture. Poverty can bring stress and make care harder to reach. Mental illness can also affect school, work, and income. This does not mean poor people are all ill, unsafe, or unable to cope. Evidence-based care uses good research, clinical judgment, and the person's needs and wishes. Talking treatments, social support, and medicines have different roles for different conditions. Better local services, care in general clinics, rights protection, less stigma, and steady funding can help. Do not assume doctors use a diagnosis called poverty syndrome or that most patients get placebos. Those claims need evidence.
groups.low: WHO's World Mental Health Report 2022 said about one in eight people had a mental disorder in 2019. That was a worldwide estimate. It does not mean one in four adults is ill now or will be ill in a lifetime. Care gaps differ by illness, country, and what is counted as care. We cannot say that only 10% of all poor patients get proven treatment. Cost, distance, and too few trained staff can block help. So can stigma, unfair treatment, or care in the wrong language. Stigma means shame or blame linked to an illness. Poverty can add stress and make care hard to reach. Illness can also make school, work, and earning harder. This does not mean poor people are all ill, dangerous, or unable to cope. Evidence-based care uses good research, a clinician's judgment, and what the person needs and wants. Talking care, social help, and medicines suit different needs. Local services, care in general clinics, rights, less stigma, and steady funds can help. Do not assume doctors use a disease label called poverty syndrome or that most people get dummy treatments. Those claims need proof.
groups.source_review: Checked WHO 2022 report and dated prevalence statement. No clinical advice specific to an individual.
groups.notes: Corrected prevalence denominator and removed fabricated uniform treatment rate, poverty syndrome, and placebo-care generalization.

groups.high: ITU's 2024 estimates placed approximately 5.5 billion people online and 2.6 billion, about 32% of the global population, offline. This is a dated measure of use, not necessarily proof that every offline person lacks network coverage. The digital divide includes infrastructure, affordability, devices, reliability, accessibility, skills, safety, and useful local-language content. Coverage alone cannot ensure meaningful participation. Someone may have a connection but lack sufficient data, a usable device, or the skills to complete an application safely. Unequal access can constrain education, employment, health information, and public services, while digital-only services can deepen exclusion. Rural and low-income communities often face larger barriers, but circumstances vary within countries and populations. Closing the divide requires infrastructure investment, affordable service, accessible design, relevant content, and practical support. Online privacy and security must be considered alongside connection rates. Offline routes to essential services remain important. Digital access can support Sustainable Development Goal 4 on education and Goal 8 on decent work and economic growth; Goal 8 is not a second education goal. Progress should be measured through useful participation, not subscriptions alone.
groups.mid: ITU estimated that 5.5 billion people used the internet in 2024. About 2.6 billion, or 32% of the world's people, were offline. These are figures for that year. Being offline does not always mean there is no network nearby. The digital divide includes network coverage, cost, devices, reliable service, access for disabled users, skills, safety, and useful content in local languages. A signal alone is not enough. Someone may be connected but lack data, a suitable phone, or the skills to fill in a form safely. This can block school, jobs, health advice, and public services. Services offered only online can leave people further behind. Rural and low-income communities often face bigger barriers, though needs vary even within a country. Better networks must go with affordable plans, accessible design, useful content, and hands-on help. Privacy and security matter too. Keep offline ways to reach essential services. Internet access can support Sustainable Development Goal 4 for education and Goal 8 for decent work and economic growth. Goal 8 is not another education goal. Judge progress by what people can safely do, not just how many accounts or subscriptions exist.
groups.low: ITU counted about 5.5 billion people online in 2024. About 2.6 billion, or 32% of the world, were offline. This is a figure for that year. An offline person may still live near a network. The problem is not just coverage. Price, a working device, reliable service, skills, safety, and language all matter. So does access for disabled people. A phone signal does not mean someone can use the internet well. They may lack data or a good device. They may need help to fill in a form safely. These gaps can block school, work, health advice, and public services. An online-only service can shut people out. Rural and poor communities often face more barriers, but needs differ within countries too. We need better networks and fair prices. We also need accessible design, local content, and practical help. People need privacy and security as well. Keep offline ways to reach key services. Internet access can help Sustainable Development Goal 4, which is about education. Goal 8 is about decent work and economic growth, not another school goal. Count what people can safely do, not just accounts and subscriptions.
groups.source_review: Checked ITU 2024 use estimates; retained year and use/coverage distinction. Intervention implications are explanatory, not causal estimates.
groups.notes: Removed unsupported binary cultural stereotypes and corrected SDG 8 definition.

groups.high: The Global Report on Food Crises 2025 reported that over 295 million people across 53 countries and territories faced high acute food insecurity in 2024. The 2024 report's roughly 282 million figure concerned 2023, so publication year and observation year must not be conflated. These crisis-country assessments are not a complete count of all chronic hunger worldwide. Conflict, economic shocks, and weather extremes can damage production, disrupt trade and assistance, displace households, and make food unaffordable. Sudan and Gaza illustrate severe conflict-related threats; disruption associated with the war in Ukraine also affected food markets. The magnitude and pathways differ by place and period. Food insecurity concerns reliable access to sufficient safe, nutritious food, not merely the quantity of grain available globally. Children, pregnant people, displaced households, and people with limited income or assets can face disproportionate nutritional risks. Effective responses combine humanitarian access, food or cash assistance where appropriate, treatment of malnutrition, livelihood support, and resilient food systems. Report-specific definitions, geographic coverage, and dates must accompany comparisons, especially when distinguishing acute food crises from chronic undernourishment.
groups.mid: The Global Report on Food Crises 2025 found that over 295 million people in 53 countries and territories faced high acute food insecurity in 2024. That means a serious short-term lack of safe access to enough food. The 2024 report's figure of about 282 million was for 2023. Check the year measured, not just the year printed on the report. These figures cover places assessed for food crises, not all long-term hunger in the world. War, economic shocks, and extreme weather can ruin crops, block trade and aid, force people from home, and raise prices beyond what families can pay. Sudan and Gaza show severe conflict-related risks. The war in Ukraine also disrupted food markets. The effects differ by time and place. Food insecurity is about getting enough safe, nutritious food reliably, not just how much grain the world grows. Children, pregnant people, displaced families, and people with little money or few assets may face greater harm. Help can include safe aid access, food or cash support where suitable, care for malnutrition, support for work and farming, and stronger food systems. Compare reports only after checking their dates, coverage, and definitions.
groups.low: The Global Report on Food Crises 2025 looked at hunger in 2024. It found over 295 million people in 53 countries and territories faced high acute food insecurity. This means a serious, short-term lack of access to enough food. The 2024 report's figure of about 282 million was for 2023. The year on the cover is not always the year counted. These reports look at places with food crises. They do not count all long-term hunger in the world. War can stop farming, trade, and aid. It can force people from home. Bad weather and economic shocks can ruin crops or make food too dear. Sudan and Gaza show grave risks from conflict. The war in Ukraine also affected food markets. Each place and time differs. Food insecurity is not just a lack of grain in the world. People must be able to get enough safe, healthy food reliably. Children, pregnant people, displaced families, and those with little money or few assets may suffer most. Help may include safe aid access, food or cash where suitable, care for malnutrition, and support for work and farms. Stronger food systems matter too. Check dates, places, and definitions before comparing figures.
groups.source_review: Checked WFP release on GRFC 2025 and report-year distinction; framed as historical crisis assessments, not latest global prevalence.
groups.notes: Corrected publication/reference-year confusion and acute-versus-chronic hunger scope.

groups.high: Microplastics are plastic particles commonly defined as smaller than five millimetres. They can arise from fragmentation of larger waste, textile fibres, tyre wear, and other sources. Humans can encounter particles through food, drinking water, and inhaled air. Particle size, shape, polymer, additives, and attached contaminants influence exposure and possible effects. Microplastics are not all PM2.5, and detecting them in food or tissue does not by itself establish a particular disease risk. WHO's 2022 review identified substantial gaps in exposure measurement, particle characterization, and evidence linking realistic exposures to health outcomes. Estimates vary with sampling, laboratory contamination controls, detection limits, and whether studies count particles or mass. No single weekly particle count or microgram estimate can be treated as a universal intake. Laboratory findings concerning inflammation or chemical effects need careful interpretation before extrapolation to humans. Uncertainty is not proof of either harmlessness or inevitable harm. Reducing plastic releases, improving waste management, and strengthening reliable research are sensible responses. Drinking-water safety should continue to prioritize established risks, including pathogens, rather than encourage unproven detoxification products or avoidance of safe water.
groups.mid: Microplastics are small plastic pieces, usually defined as less than five millimetres across. They can come from larger plastic breaking up, clothes shedding fibres, tyre wear, and other sources. People can take them in through food, drinking water, and air. Size, shape, plastic type, added chemicals, and dirt on the pieces can affect exposure and possible harm. Not all microplastics are fine PM2.5 dust. Finding plastic in food or a tissue sample does not prove it caused a disease. WHO's 2022 review found major gaps in measuring exposure and linking real-life doses to health effects. Studies use different tests and size limits. Samples can also be contaminated in the lab. Counting pieces is not the same as weighing them. So there is no single proven weekly amount that everyone takes in. Lab findings about inflammation or chemicals do not directly show what happens in people. Uncertainty does not mean the particles are harmless, or that harm is certain. Reduce plastic releases, improve waste handling, and support careful research. For drinking water, keep dealing with proven dangers such as germs. Do not replace safe water with unproven detox products or unsafe alternatives.
groups.low: Microplastics are small bits of plastic, usually under five millimetres wide. They can come from old plastic breaking up, fibres from clothes, worn tyres, and other sources. People can take them in through food, water, or air. Their size, shape, plastic type, added chemicals, and dirt can all matter. They are not all the fine dust called PM2.5. Finding plastic in food or body tissue does not prove it caused illness. WHO's 2022 review found big gaps in what we know about doses and health effects. Studies test in different ways and miss different sizes. Plastic can also get into a sample in the lab. A count of pieces is not the same as their weight. There is no fixed weekly amount that applies to us all. A lab test showing swelling or chemical effects is not direct proof of harm in people. We cannot say all plastic is safe, or that harm is certain. Cut plastic waste and leaks. Improve waste care and careful research. Safe drinking water is still vital. Known risks such as germs need control. Do not stop drinking safe water or buy unproven detox products because of these claims.
groups.source_review: Checked WHO exposure review and drinking-water review. Distinguishes hazard hypotheses from established human outcomes.
groups.notes: Removed unsupported intake count, universal PM2.5 classification, fixed source fraction, and asserted clinical effects.

groups.high: An urban heat island occurs when built-up areas are warmer than nearby less-developed areas. The magnitude depends on surface versus air measurements, time, season, weather, and local design. EPA summarizes US studies showing urban air temperatures about 1–7°F higher by day and 2–5°F higher at night; these are not universal differences of 5–7°C. Dark surfaces can absorb sunlight, while roofs, roads, and buildings store and release heat. Less vegetation and available moisture reduce cooling through evapotranspiration. Street geometry can limit airflow or alter heat exchange, and vehicles, industry, and air conditioning release additional heat. Absorbed sunlight is not automatically converted into latent heat; latent heat is associated with processes such as evaporation. Heat islands can increase cooling demand and health risks, especially for people without safe cooling, shade, or adequate housing. Trees, shade, suitable reflective roofs and pavements, vegetation, and locally appropriate urban design can help. Measures require context: glare, water supply, maintenance, and effects on pedestrians must be considered. A single citywide temperature average can hide substantial neighborhood inequalities.
groups.mid: A heat island is a built-up area that is warmer than the less-developed land nearby. The gap depends on whether you measure air or surfaces. Time, season, weather, and city design matter too. EPA's summary of US studies gives daytime air differences of about 1–7°F and night differences of 2–5°F. It does not say every city is 5–7°C hotter. Dark roads and roofs absorb sunlight. Buildings and paving store heat and release it later. With fewer plants and less water, there is less cooling by evaporation and plant moisture loss, called evapotranspiration. Streets can change airflow, while traffic, industry, and air conditioning add waste heat. Sunlight absorbed by a road does not all become latent heat; that term refers to energy in changes such as water evaporating. Heat islands can raise cooling bills and harm health. People without shade, safe cooling, or good homes face greater risks. Trees, shade, suitable light-reflecting roofs and paving, plants, and better design may help. Plans must consider glare, water needs, upkeep, and people walking nearby. One average for a city can hide much hotter neighborhoods.
groups.low: A city area can be warmer than nearby open land. This is a heat island. The gap changes with weather, time, season, and city design. It also matters if we measure air or a surface. EPA's US studies found air gaps of about 1–7°F by day and 2–5°F at night. This is not a rule that all cities are 5–7°C hotter. Dark roads and roofs soak up sunlight. Buildings and paving store heat and let it out later. Fewer plants and less water mean less cooling as water turns to vapour. Plant moisture loss is part of evapotranspiration. Street shape can block airflow. Cars, factories, and air conditioners add heat too. Heat stored in a road is not all latent heat. That term includes energy used when water evaporates. More heat can raise cooling costs and harm health. People without shade, safe cooling, or good homes may suffer more. Trees, shade, plants, and suitable roofs or paving that reflect light can help. Good design matters too. Plans must check glare, water use, upkeep, and effects on people walking. An average for a whole city can hide much hotter streets and homes.
groups.source_review: Checked EPA's air/surface distinctions, Fahrenheit ranges, mechanisms, and mitigation framework.
groups.notes: Corrected Fahrenheit/Celsius conflation and latent-heat explanation; qualified context-dependent temperature differences.

groups.high: The ILO, Walk Free, and IOM Global Estimates of Modern Slavery published in 2022 estimated that 49.6 million people experienced forced labour or forced marriage on any given day in 2021. Approximately 27.6 million were in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage. About 3.3 million people in forced labour were children, roughly one in eight of the forced-labour total, not 42%. Fifty million people is not 10% of the global population. The categories concern coercion, not simply any low-paid work or every form of child labour. Threats, debt bondage, retained identity documents, restrictions on movement, and abuse of vulnerability can prevent people from leaving. Migrant workers and people with limited protection can face heightened risks, though exploitation occurs across regions and income groups. Responses include enforcing labour rights, regulating recruitment, protecting safe reporting, remedy and survivor support, and addressing forced marriage with appropriate rights-based measures. Enforcement should not punish victims for seeking help. Historical estimates are uncertain and not equivalent to real-time counts. Prevention and assistance require attention to safety, children's needs, and the different mechanisms of labour and marriage coercion.
groups.mid: ILO, Walk Free, and IOM published their modern slavery estimates in 2022. They estimated that 49.6 million people were in forced labour or forced marriage on a given day in 2021. About 27.6 million were in forced labour, and 22 million in forced marriage. About 3.3 million forced-labour victims were children. That is roughly one in eight, not 42%. Nor is 50 million 10% of the world's population. These figures concern coercion: people cannot freely refuse or leave. They do not count all low-paid jobs or all child labour as the same thing. Threats, debt, withheld identity papers, blocked movement, and abuse of vulnerability can trap people. Migrant workers and those with little protection may face greater risks, but exploitation occurs in rich and poor places. Action can include labour-law enforcement, fair recruitment rules, safe reporting, remedies, and support for survivors. Forced marriage also needs its own rights-based response. Victims should not be punished for asking for help. These are historical estimates, not exact live counts. Help must protect safety and meet children's needs, while recognizing that forced work and forced marriage involve different forms of control.
groups.low: ILO, Walk Free, and IOM released a report in 2022. It estimated that 49.6 million people were in forced labour or forced marriage on a given day in 2021: 27.6 million in forced labour and 22 million in forced marriage. Of those in forced labour, 3.3 million were children, about one in eight, not 42%. Fifty million is not 10% of the world. The key is force or control: people cannot freely say no or leave, so a low-paid job alone is not the same thing. Not all child labour is counted in this figure. Threats, debt, taking identity papers, or stopping someone moving can trap them. Those with little protection, including some migrant workers, face more risk. This happens in rich and poor places. Enforce labour rights and fair rules for recruiters. Give people safe ways to report, seek a remedy, and get support. Forced marriage needs steps suited to it too. Do not punish victims for seeking help. These are estimates for a past year, not exact counts today, and safety and children's needs come first. Forced work and forced marriage do not always use the same kinds of control.
groups.source_review: Checked 2022 publication covering 2021 and ILO forced-labour child count.
groups.notes: Corrected observation year, absurd population percentage, child percentage, and conflation of all exploitation categories.

groups.high: Wealth is the stock of assets minus debts, whereas income is a flow over a period. Shares must be compared using the same year, population, asset definition, and valuation method. Oxfam's September 2024 analysis reported that the richest 1% owned 43% of global financial assets. This is not automatically 43% of all wealth. The World Inequality Report 2022 estimated that the global top 10% held 76% of household wealth and the bottom 50% held 2% under its principal valuation; market-exchange-rate estimates showed still greater concentration. These are distinct statistics, not interchangeable proof that the top 1% holds 42–44% of total wealth while the bottom half holds exactly 0.5%. Asset-price growth, inheritance, savings opportunities, debt, and taxation can affect concentration and mobility. Aggregate shares alone cannot prove a specific causal mechanism or inevitable social outcome. People with little net wealth generally have smaller buffers against job loss or price shocks. Policy options include public services, access to education and assets, and tax design, each requiring assessment of distributional and other effects. Transparent definitions matter more than combining striking but incompatible figures.
groups.mid: Wealth means what you own minus what you owe. Income means what you receive over time. To compare shares, use the same year, people, kinds of assets, and method of valuation. Oxfam reported in September 2024 that the richest 1% owned 43% of global financial assets. Financial assets are not the same as all wealth. The World Inequality Report 2022 found that the richest 10% held 76% of household wealth and the poorest half held 2% under its main method. Using market exchange rates showed even greater inequality. These are different measures that do not prove that the top 1% owns 42–44% of all wealth while the bottom half has exactly 0.5%. Asset prices, inheritance, chances to save, debt, and taxes can affect wealth gaps and movement between groups. The shares alone do not prove which cause matters most or that one social result is certain. People with little net wealth have less to fall back on after losing work or facing price rises. Public services, access to education and assets, and tax rules are possible policy responses. Their effects need assessment, and definitions must remain clear instead of mixing dramatic figures from different measures.
groups.low: Wealth is what you own minus what you owe. Income is money you receive over time. They are not the same. Compare figures only if the year, people, assets, and way of valuing them match. In September 2024, Oxfam said the richest 1% owned 43% of global financial assets. That is not all wealth. The World Inequality Report 2022 said the richest 10% held 76% of household wealth. The poorest half held 2% under its main method. A method using market exchange rates showed an even wider gap. These figures count different things. They do not prove the top 1% owns 42–44% of all wealth, or that the bottom half has exactly 0.5%. Rising asset prices, money passed down in families, savings chances, debt, and taxes can affect the gap. Shares alone do not tell us the main cause or a certain future. People with few assets after debts have less to fall back on if they lose work or prices rise. Better public services, access to education and assets, and changes to tax rules may help. Check their effects. Clear definitions matter more than mixing striking numbers that do not match.
groups.source_review: Checked directly published Oxfam and World Inequality Lab statistics with named dates and asset concepts. Did not invent a 2026 estimate.
groups.notes: Corrected financial-assets/total-wealth conflation and reversed poor-household consumption claim; removed unsupported universal causal conclusions.

groups.high: Automated hiring systems can disadvantage qualified applicants when resume parsing, scoring, or selection criteria do not reliably measure job-relevant ability. Unusual layouts, columns, images, or inaccessible formats may cause information-extraction failures; this need not mean a trained model deliberately penalizes creativity. Historical data can also reproduce unequal opportunities, while proxy features may correlate with protected characteristics. These are potential mechanisms, not proof of a particular unnamed case or a universal rejection percentage. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework emphasizes context, measurement, governance, and management of harmful bias. In the United States, existing discrimination and disability law can apply when employers use automated tools; buying software does not remove responsibility. Employers should test parsing across formats, validate criteria against actual job needs, examine subgroup outcomes, provide suitable accommodations and accessible alternatives, and enable meaningful review of errors. Human oversight is useful only if reviewers have evidence and authority to act. Applicants can use readable formats and seek review when information is lost, but fairness must not depend solely on applicants guessing a hidden system's preferences. Accuracy and accessibility must be evaluated together.
groups.mid: Hiring software can miss qualified people if it reads resumes badly or scores things that do not show job ability. Columns, images, unusual layouts, or inaccessible files may stop a parser from finding skills. That is not always a model deciding that creativity is bad. Past hiring data can also repeat unfair patterns. Other features may act as indirect signals of a protected trait. These are possible risks, not proof of an unnamed case or a fixed rejection rate. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework calls for attention to context, testing, governance, and harmful bias. In the US, discrimination and disability laws can still apply when employers use software. Buying a tool does not remove their duty. Employers should test different resume formats, check that scores reflect job needs, compare results across groups, provide suitable accommodations and accessible options, and let people challenge errors. A human reviewer needs evidence and power to fix a problem, not just a title. Applicants can use readable files and ask for review if details are lost. But fair hiring should not depend on guessing secret software preferences. Test accuracy and access together.
groups.low: Hiring software can miss a good worker. It may fail to read a resume or score things that do not show skill for the job. Columns, pictures, unusual layouts, or hard-to-access files may hide key details from a parser. This is not always AI choosing to reject creativity. Old hiring records can also teach unfair patterns. A feature may act as a clue to a protected trait. These are risks, not proof of an unnamed case or a fixed rate of rejection. NIST's AI Risk Management Framework calls for context, tests, clear duties, and checks on harmful bias. US discrimination and disability laws can still apply when software is used. An employer cannot pass all blame to the tool. Test how it reads different resumes. Check that scores match job needs and that groups are treated fairly. Offer suitable accommodations and accessible choices. Let people challenge errors. A human reviewer needs facts and the power to fix mistakes. An applicant can use a clear file and ask for review if skills were missed. But fair access should not depend on guessing hidden software rules. Check both accuracy and access.
